Many Hats
Resume

Open-source agent system

Agreement was easy. Accountability needed a structure.

I built Many Hats to give AI-assisted product work distinct roles, shared facts, and an independent critic. The human remains accountable for the decision.

Role
Author
Scope
Thirteen agents and fifteen portable skills
Key decision
Separate roles, practice, knowledge, and project work
Outcome
Public v0.1 and a replayable, fictional Library Holds demo

I — Inspiration

Strategy and product rules arrived as one voice

When one agent frames the opportunity, defines the product, and reviews its own recommendation, a confident answer can conceal several different responsibilities. Many Hats began with the need to make those responsibilities visible and keep the consequential decision with the human.

Design Dash contained 53 stage-oriented methods. They worked in facilitated workshops, but ongoing product work needed clearer responsibility: someone to frame the problem, someone to define the domain, and someone to challenge the plan.

I reviewed public agent collections for role boundaries and verification patterns, then wrote original contracts for the team. Each role has a defined job, evidence expectations, and limits on what it can approve.

D — Design Process

Stable roles needed a place apart from project work

I separated stable roles from reusable skills, shared product facts, and project deliverables. This makes a correction easier to route. A product-specific rule stays with that project; a reusable practice change needs a motivating case, evaluation, and human approval.

The shared object library belongs in Knowledge, where every role can cite it. The domain specialist stewards it. Projects can reference or fork an object without silently rewriting it for everyone else.

I mapped the 53 Design Dash methods to accountable roles and consolidated them into fifteen portable skills. The original methods remain as references.

E — Engagement

Let the critic keep its independence

The fictional Library Holds demonstration made the challenge and the response inspectable. The independent critic reviewed the proposed direction without inheriting responsibility for delivering it.

This is a demonstration of collaboration contracts, not a claim that simulated agreement replaces feedback from users or specialists. The human owns the tradeoffs and external actions. Each role prepares evidence and recommendations within a defined responsibility, so a challenge can remain visible even after the direction is accepted.

A — Action

The critic challenged features the MVP didn’t need

Library Holds is a fictional demo of a holds-and-pickup workflow. The tempting scope included branch transfers, waitlist incentives, and a notification preference center. The core problem was simpler: patrons needed to know when a book was ready and when to collect it.

The product lead proposed a small Hold MVP. The domain specialist defined Hold, Patron, Item, and Pickup Window. Flow and content roles worked from that model. The independent critic challenged the extra features; the accepted direction cited that challenge and left them out.

S — Success

v0.1 made the approach public and replayable

v0.1 is public and cloneable. A builder can replay the demo from direction through objects, flow, language, and independent review. Host adapters change how tools discover the skills, not their contracts.

I have no adoption count, and the demo is not a field study. The repository demonstrates the architecture: a specialist leaves a citable artifact, stays within its role, and keeps approval with the human owner.
